title: Implementation and Operational Research
venue: JAIDS Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes
abstract: The objective of this study was to quantify the impact of a new technology to communicate the results of an infant HIV diagnostic test on test turnaround time and to quantify the association between late delivery of test results and patient loss to follow-up. We used data collected during a pilot implementation of Global Package Radio Service (GPRS) printers for communicating results in the early infant diagnosis program in Mozambique from 2008 through 2010. Our dataset comprised 1757 patient records, of which 767 were from before implementation and 990 from after implementation of expedited results delivery system. We used multivariate logistic regression model to determine the association between late result delivery (more than 30 days between sample collection and result delivery to the health facility) and the probability of result collection by the infant's caregiver. We used a sample selection model to determine the association between late result delivery to the facility and further delay in collection of results by the caregiver. The mean test turnaround time reduced from 68.13 to 41.05 days post-expedited results delivery system. Caregivers collected only 665 (37.8%) of the 1757 results. After controlling for confounders, the late delivery of results was associated with a reduction of approximately 18% (0.44 vs. 0.36; P < 0.01) in the probability of results collected by the caregivers (odds ratio = 0.67, P < 0.05). Late delivery of results was also associated with a further average increase in 20.91 days of delay in collection of results (P < 0.01). Early infant diagnosis program managers should further evaluate the cost-effectiveness of operational interventions (eg, GPRS printers) that reduce delays.

summary.oneLiner: Expediting HIV test results using GPRS printers reduces turnaround time and significantly increases the probability of caregivers collecting those critical test results.
summary.overview: This study examines the effectiveness of using GPRS printers to speed up the communication of infant HIV test results in Mozambique. The researchers found that implementing this technology cut wait times for test results by over 25 days. They observed that faster delivery significantly improves the chances that caregivers will actually collect the results, whereas delayed delivery leads to higher patient loss. Ultimately, the study highlights how operational improvements in diagnostic processes can directly influence clinical engagement.
summary.question: What is the impact of using GPRS printers on HIV test turnaround time, and how does the delay in result delivery affect the likelihood of caregivers collecting those results?
summary.method: The researchers employed a multivariate logistic regression model and a sample selection model to analyze the relationship between result delivery times and caregiver collection behavior.
summary.data: 1,757 patient records from an early infant diagnosis program in Mozambique between 2008 and 2010 (767 pre-implementation and 990 post-implementation).
findings: Implementation of an expedited results delivery system reduced mean test turnaround time from 68.13 to 41.05 days.
Late delivery of results (more than 30 days) is associated with an 18% reduction in the probability of caregivers collecting the results.
Late delivery of results is associated with an additional average delay of 20.91 days in result collection by caregivers.
summary.whyItMatters: The findings suggest that operational interventions, such as GPRS-enabled reporting, can play a critical role in public health by mitigating administrative bottlenecks that cause patients to drop out of care systems.
